The blanket labels like realist, anti-realist, irrealist can get exhausted pretty quickly, imo. If we're accepting substance dualism, I'd suppose I'm a nominalist. I believe numbers are a symbolic representation of what ultimately boils down to cognitive significance - the problem being, cognitive significance is a great mystery. There are different reasons to utilize the concept of number depending on what the source of significance is in the system we are trying to study, or the phenomenon under study. On this view, mathematics becomes the simplest and most abstract way to view anything in the universe, and it depends crucially on the observer/studier to pick out the fundamental unit of significance.

For example, take an apple tree. When we perceive an object like an apple, a good deal of questions are raised about just what an apple is. At root, we'd be inclined to count apples - that is, the magnitude of the collection of apples - because they have a certain kind of significance to us when taken at the level of the unit apple. But in reality, one apple and whether it is, in fact, one thing is up for debate - I see it as depending entirely on the frame of reference, our relationship as embodied things to that apple, and the significance is gains as one thing, versus a collection of millions of atoms, for instance. It would be very cumbersome to refer to this individual unit of significance - the apple - as: "Hey, hand me that collection of 3 trillion atoms arranged in such a way that the physical low level facts make it appear to us like a tasty, red, quasi-orb." What comes to bear on us, what strikes us, is the significance that emerges once it has the structure and when that structure interacts with our perceptual machinery the way that it does.

So we call it 'one' apple. That designation is arbitrary, it's based on the human embodied relationship to it. The idea of numbering an apple would make no intelligible sense to something like a bacterium, or to God. Because, since that unit has a certain way that it comes to bear on us, we find it useful to know things like the magnitude of apples we could get from a tree, we number them. That's useful, because as the sophistication of our contacts with - and knowledge about - apple trees grows, we can cause the tree to generate more significance for us, in part because we are now quantifying over that significance with numbers. We learn that doing this with the fertilizer causes the number of apples to grow by 2x, for example.

There seem to be, at the base of reality, certain primitive categories that form of fundamental entities in physics: mass, energy, motion, direction, and time. The way these things interact determines what has cognitive significance on the basis of for who's sake we are observing.

I see the numberals as symbolic containers for abstract ideas. I don't believe they exist in reality; they require a relationship involving an observer. It's hard for me to believe that there is a number in reality specified by the symbol '2' that exists whether I am capable of knowing it or not. It's interesting to think that the concept of quantification is probably universal though. It is hard to imagine, in a possible world involving an alien life form of sufficient intelligence, that it would not have concepts for measuring and counting. So in some odd way, the ideas are real, they are observer dependent, but we'd expect any sufficiently intelligent thing to organize it's representation of reality into countable units (depsite the fact it's symbols for {1, 2, 3.........n} might look completely different). Does this mean numbers are materially real? What does it mean to be conceptually and not materially real?

A person like me wants to say that this somehow breaks down to the primitive nature of ANY conscious experience, which is that the form of experience itself involves identifying one or more things within the field of experience as significant. Hence, the experience itself scaffolds every reason you could have for counting things. To me, this primitive form of experience comes first, that is to say, the tendency for any conscious experience to be formed by the condensation of reality into something significant that occupies our attention/awareness. The quantification comes later, and only roughly at first. Two enemies approaching my from either side has a different significance than one approaching from directly in front of me.

The a priori and a posteriori distinction becomes relevant here, especially from a developmental standpoint. I think it is very reasonable to imagine that evolution has favored the development of brain structures in which a certain intelligible quantifying framework already exists in any human being born. Of course, those rough concepts get more content as we get older and are educated, but primitive ideas about quantity are already there. Infants know when their counterparts on the floor next to them have something (or more or less of that thing) that they don't. But again, it all comes back to cognitive significance for me.

Why should anything have an experience of something as being significant for them? That answer would be the more philosophically interesting one for me personally.
